subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Ugly Food Movement
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Ugly Food Movement.

hook.text: Supermarkets reject up to 40% of produce for being the wrong size, shape, or color.

buildup.text: Curved cucumbers, spotted apples, and small potatoes never reach the shelf.

discovery.text: They taste identical. Cosmetic standards create billions of kilograms of perfectly edible waste.

twist.text: Companies like Imperfect Foods now sell ugly produce at a discount, building a market for it.

climax.text: France banned supermarkets from throwing away unsold food — it must be donated or composted.

punchline.text: A crooked carrot feeds you just as well as a straight one.

quiz.question: Why do supermarkets reject a large portion of produce?
options: Cosmetic standards on size, shape, and color

details.summary: The ugly food movement fights food waste by promoting the sale and consumption of cosmetically imperfect produce. Initiatives include discounted ugly produce boxes, relaxed supermarket appearance standards.
details.whyItMatters: Up to 40 percent of produce is discarded for purely cosmetic reasons. The ugly food movement addresses a massive source of waste by changing perceptions rather than technology.
takeaways: Up to 40 percent of produce is rejected for cosmetic defects
Ugly produce subscriptions sell imperfect food at discount
Changing consumer expectations directly reduces farm-level waste

faq.question: Is ugly produce as nutritious as perfect-looking produce?
faq.answer: Yes. Shape, size, and surface blemishes have no effect on nutritional content or taste. An oddly shaped carrot or a spotted apple provides the same vitamins, minerals, and fiber as its cosmetically perfect counterpart.

faq.question: How successful are ugly produce programs?
faq.answer: Companies like Imperfect Foods and services from major retailers have diverted millions of kilograms of produce from waste. France pioneered intermarche's inglorious fruits and vegetables campaign, which went viral and inspired similar efforts worldwide.
